title: Linear-time exact inversion counting
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm that, for every \(n\ge2\) and every explicitly listed permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]\), computes \(\operatorname{Inv}(\pi)=|\{(i,j):1\le i<j\le n,\ \pi(i)>\pi(j)\}|\) exactly in \(O(n)\) worst-case time?
definitions: The input contains \(n\) and the array \(\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(n)\), promised to contain each integer from one through \(n\) exactly once. The output is the single integer inversion count, between zero and \(n(n-1)/2\). Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Choose \(d\ge3\), so the count fits in a word. All constants are independent of the permutation and \(n\). No randomness is allowed. The values are already ranks, so no conversion from arbitrary ordered keys is required.

context_blocks.text: An inversion counts an out-of-order pair in a ranking. The exact total is also the Kendall tau distance from the identity ordering and the minimum number of adjacent swaps needed to sort the permutation.
Chan and Pătraşcu give an \(O(n\sqrt{\log n})\) exact word-RAM algorithm and a linear-time constant-relative-error approximation. The latter does not compute the exact count.
The input is a permutation of small integers, so sorting those integers itself is already easy. Determining how many pairs were out of order is a separate offline aggregation problem.

The linear exact endpoint is an editorial formulation of the remaining gap. The September 2026 search found no general exact linear algorithm, but the status evidence relies mainly on older primary work and is weaker than for the other additions.

why: A simple central offline counting task exposes a basic gap in the power of word-RAM algorithms, despite having only one output value and already rank-compressed input.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the specified model, quantifiers and guarantees. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean; a partial improvement does not meet the target.

references.title: Counting Inversions, Offline Orthogonal Range Counting, and Related Problems
references.locator: SODA 2010; author manuscript 7 July 2009; sections 1.1–1.2, Corollary 2.2 and section 4.

references.title: Counting inversions adaptively
references.locator: Introduction and adaptive bound; uses the Chan–Pătraşcu exact algorithm.

progress.text: Exact counting takes \(O(n\sqrt{\log n})\), while constant-relative-error approximation takes linear time.
Adaptive bounds improve performance on inputs with fewer inversions, without an exact linear worst-case guarantee for all permutations.

The linear endpoint is editorial rather than an attributed conjecture; present-status review remains limited by older direct evidence.

sentences: An inversion is a pair of positions that appear in the wrong relative order in a permutation.
The task is to compute the exact total number of inversions.
The question asks for deterministic linear time on a word RAM with logarithmic words.
Linear approximation and faster algorithms for nearly sorted inputs do not give this exact worst-case guarantee.
The current-status review is limited mainly to older primary evidence, and the card records that uncertainty.
